args.text:
The lighthouse keeper had not slept in three days. Not because of the storm, though the storm was real—three nights of wind that turned the sea into a wall of grey teeth. Not because of the light, though the light had flickered twice and he’d climbed the spiral stairs with bleeding fingers to relight the wick. He hadn’t slept because of the sound.

It came from below the waterline. A low, rhythmic thumping, like a heart the size of a house beating against the rocks. It had started on the first night, faint as a whisper. By the second night, it was a drum. By the third, it was a voice, though not a voice he could parse into words. Just a sound that meant *here, here, I am here, and I am not alone, and neither are you.*

Elias had been the keeper for eleven years. He knew the sound of every wave, every gull, every creak of the tower’s iron bones. He knew the particular groan the foundation made when the tide pulled at its roots. But he did not know this sound. It was older than the tower. Older, he suspected, than the island itself.

On the morning of the fourth day, the storm broke. The sky peeled open like a wound, and the sea went flat and silver. Elias stood on the gallery, his coat soaked through, and looked down at the water. The thumping had stopped. In its place, something else: a silence so complete it had texture, like velvet pressed against the eardrums.

Then he saw it.

A shape, vast and dark, rising slowly from the shallows. Not a whale. Not a rock. Something with the suggestion of a form, the way a dream has the suggestion of a face. It moved with a patience that made Elias’s knees go soft. It did not approach the tower. It did not need to. It simply existed, and in its existence, the thumping returned—gentler now, almost tender, like a hand on a shoulder.

Elias understood, then, what it had been saying all along. Not a warning. Not a threat. A question, asked in the only language the deep could speak: *Are you still there? Are you still watching? Do you still see me?*

He raised his hand. Not a wave. A confirmation. *Yes. I see you. I am here.*

The shape sank back into the silver water. The thumping faded. The silence returned, but it was no longer empty. It was full, the way a held breath is full, the way a promise is full.

Elias went inside. He lit the lamp. He climbed the stairs. And for the first time in three days, he slept. Not because the storm had passed. Not because the light was steady. But because he had answered, and the answer had been enough.

args.text:
The lighthouse keeper had not slept in three days. Not because of the storm, though the storm was real—three nights of wind that turned the sea into a wall of grey teeth. Not because of the light, though the light had flickered twice and he’d climbed the spiral stairs with bleeding fingers to relight the wick. He hadn’t slept because of the sound.

It came from below the waterline. A low, rhythmic thumping, like a heart the size of a house beating against the rocks. It had started on the first night, faint as a whisper. By the second night, it was a drum. By the third, it was a voice, though not a voice he could parse into words. Just a sound that meant *here, here, I am here, and I am not alone, and neither are you.*

Elias had been the keeper for eleven years. He knew the sound of every wave, every gull, every creak of the tower’s iron bones. He knew the particular groan the foundation made when the tide pulled at its roots. But he did not know this sound. It was older than the tower. Older, he suspected, than the island itself.

On the morning of the fourth day, the storm broke. The sky peeled open like a wound, and the sea went flat and silver. Elias stood on the gallery, his coat soaked through, and looked down at the water. The thumping had stopped. In its place, something else: a silence so complete it had texture, like velvet pressed against the eardrums.

Then he saw it.

A shape, vast and dark, rising slowly from the shallows. Not a whale. Not a rock. Something with the suggestion of a form, the way a dream has the suggestion of a face. It moved with a patience that made Elias’s knees go soft. It did not approach the tower. It did not need to. It simply existed, and in its existence, the thumping returned—gentler now, almost tender, like a hand on a shoulder.

Elias understood, then, what it had been saying all along. Not a warning. Not a threat. A question, asked in the only language the deep could speak: *Are you still there? Are you still watching? Do you still see me?*

He raised his hand. Not a wave. A confirmation. *Yes. I see you. I am here.*

The shape sank back into the silver water. The thumping faded. The silence returned, but it was no longer empty. It was full, the way a held breath is full, the way a promise is full.

Elias went inside. He lit the lamp. He climbed the stairs. And for the first time in three days, he slept. Not because the storm had passed. Not because the light was steady. But because he had answered, and the answer had been enough.
